title: Feathers in the Wind
summary: Dudu hears an embarrassing secret about a boy in his class, and the words are already tickling his tongue. Grandpa takes him up to the roof with an old pillow and shows him how hard it is to gather words once they leave your mouth. A story about gossip, the power of words, and choosing to speak kindly.
pages:
At recess, by the water fountain, Roni pulled Dudu aside and whispered:
"Guess what I heard? Gil still sleeps with the light on, because he's scared of the dark!"
Roni giggled. Dudu giggled too, but something in his tummy squeezed up a little.

All the way home, the secret popped around in Dudu's mouth like popping candy.
He almost told Noa from his building. He almost told Shira, who goes to his after-school class.
It was so exciting to tell! And what could happen? It was only one sentence.

That evening, Grandpa came for dinner.
"Grandpa," Dudu began, "want to hear something funny about Gil from my class?"
Grandpa put down his fork. "Is it something Gil would be happy for me to tell everyone?"
Dudu was quiet. "Not exactly," he mumbled.

"This Shabbat we read Parashat Metzora," said Grandpa. "The sages say the word 'metzora' hints at someone who spreads bad talk about others.
The Torah takes our words very seriously.
Come, I want to show you something."

Grandpa took an old pillow from the closet and went up to the roof with Dudu.
A cool evening breeze was blowing.
Grandpa snipped the pillow open with scissors and said, "Now, shake it hard."
Dudu stared at him in amazement. "Really? Mom will be angry!"
Grandpa smiled. "It's my pillow. Shake."

Dudu shook. Hundreds of white feathers flew out.
They flew over the roof, floated above the trees, and landed on the neighbors' balconies and on the cars in the street.
Dudu laughed. It looked like snow.

"Very nice," said Grandpa. "And now, gather them all back into the pillow."
"What?" Dudu's eyes went wide. "But they're everywhere! Some already flew to the next street!"
He tried to catch a few feathers, but the wind only blew them farther away.

Grandpa sat down beside him on the railing.
"That's how it is with words," he said quietly. "It's very easy to scatter them, with just one puff.
But once they're out, you can't gather them back. They pass from one person to the next, and reach places we never even thought of."

Dudu thought about Gil. About how he sometimes sits alone at recess.
He imagined the whole class laughing at him, and Gil blushing right up to his ears.
"Grandpa," he said, "I don't want my words to be feathers like that."

The next day, by the water fountain, Roni came over again. "Did you tell anyone about Gil?"
"No," said Dudu, "and I'm not going to. Sometimes I get scared in the dark too."
Roni looked at him for a moment. "Actually," he admitted, "me too."

At the next recess, Dudu sat down next to Gil.
"Want to play dodgeball with me?" he asked.
Gil smiled a big smile. And Dudu felt his tummy, which had squeezed up yesterday, open up now like a soft, cozy pillow.

Our words can fly far, too.
We can scatter words that hurt, or we can scatter good words: a compliment, a "thank you," a "come play with us."
So which good words will we scatter tomorrow?
